lesson.title: Blocking the Door: How Competitive Inhibitors Outcompete Substrates
lesson.summary: Competitive inhibitors mimic a substrate closely enough to occupy an enzyme's active site, and because they compete for the same site, raising substrate concentration can restore normal reaction rates.
lesson.body:
Every enzyme's power comes from its active site, the precisely shaped pocket where a substrate binds to form the enzyme-substrate complex before catalysis lowers the activation energy of a reaction. That precision is also a vulnerability. If another molecule happens to share enough of the substrate's size, shape, and chemical groups, it can slip into the same active site and simply sit there, occupying the pocket without being converted into product. This is the basic idea behind competitive inhibition: a molecule that competes with the natural substrate for the same binding site on the enzyme.

Because the inhibitor and the substrate are fighting for the identical piece of binding space, the outcome depends on concentration. If substrate is abundant relative to inhibitor, substrate molecules will win most of the competitions for the active site by sheer numbers, and the enzyme still reaches its normal maximum reaction rate, just more slowly than it would with no inhibitor present. Add enough substrate and you can outcompete the inhibitor almost entirely, which is the defining signature of competitive inhibition: raising substrate concentration overcomes it. This distinguishes it from inhibitors that bind somewhere other than the active site, which added substrate cannot dislodge.

A textbook example is malonate's effect on succinate dehydrogenase, an enzyme of the citric acid cycle that normally converts succinate into fumarate. Malonate's structure resembles succinate closely enough to bind the active site, but its structure is wrong for the reaction to proceed, so it simply blocks the site and stalls the enzyme. Because the binding is reversible and noncovalent, held together by the same weak interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions, and van der Waals contacts, that normally position a real substrate, the inhibitor can also let go, especially when true substrate concentration rises.

This same logic underlies several important drugs. Statins lower cholesterol by competitively inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that catalyzes the committed step of cholesterol synthesis, and methotrexate treats cancer and autoimmune disease by mimicking folate closely enough to competitively block dihydrofolate reductase, starving rapidly dividing cells of the folate derivatives they need to make DNA. In both cases, chemists designed a molecule specifically to resemble the natural substrate well enough to occupy the active site without ever being processed into product.

Understanding competitive inhibition also matters for how scientists describe enzyme behavior quantitatively. It leaves an enzyme's maximum possible reaction rate unchanged, because enough substrate can always win out eventually, but it makes the enzyme behave as though it has a weaker affinity for substrate, since more substrate is now needed to reach any given reaction rate. That combination, unchanged maximum rate paired with an apparently reduced substrate affinity, is the kinetic fingerprint that lets researchers identify competitive inhibition experimentally and distinguish it from the allosteric mechanisms covered next.
